ramayana-2-58-15.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-58-16.translation: 'When the arrow was drawn out, he went to heaven right there, grieving for you both, lamenting that you are blind.'
ramayana-2-58-16.meaning: The son's last thought was for his parents.
ramayana-2-58-16.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-58-17.translation: 'Through ignorance I suddenly struck your son. Whatever remains to be done now, may the sage be gracious to me.'
ramayana-2-58-17.meaning: He places himself at the sage's mercy.
ramayana-2-58-17.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-58-18.translation: Hearing those cruel words, sighing and wasted by grief, the sage of great power spoke to me as I stood with folded hands.
ramayana-2-58-18.meaning: The father responds to the confession.
ramayana-2-58-18.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-58-19.translation: 'King, if you had not told me of this evil deed yourself, your head would at once have burst into a hundred thousand pieces.'
ramayana-2-58-19.meaning: Honest confession saved him from immediate destruction.
ramayana-2-58-19.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-58-20.translation: 'King, the killing of a forest-dwelling ascetic by a Kshatriya, done knowingly, would cast down even Indra from his place.'
ramayana-2-58-20.meaning: Deliberately harming a hermit is a terrible sin.
ramayana-2-58-20.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-58-21.translation: 'Because this was done in ignorance, you live. Otherwise today the whole family of the Raghavas would perish, let alone you.'
ramayana-2-58-21.meaning: Intention matters greatly in judging an act.
ramayana-2-58-21.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-58-22.translation: He said to me, 'King, take us to that place. Today we wish to see our son for the last time.'
ramayana-2-58-22.meaning: The parents ask to see their son.
ramayana-2-58-22.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-58-23.translation: '...his body covered in blood, his deerskin garment scattered, lying senseless on the ground, gone into the power of the king of dharma.'
ramayana-2-58-23.meaning: They will find their son dead.
ramayana-2-58-23.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-58-24.translation: Then I alone led the deeply grieving pair to that place and let the sage and his wife touch their son.
ramayana-2-58-24.meaning: He guides the blind parents to their son's body.
ramayana-2-58-24.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-58-25.translation: The two ascetics, touching their son and reaching him, fell upon his body, and his father said this.
ramayana-2-58-25.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-58-26.translation: 'Am I not dear to you, son? Look at your mother, righteous one. Why do you not embrace me, son? Speak, gentle one.'
ramayana-2-58-26.meaning: A father's heartbroken plea to his dead child.
ramayana-2-58-26.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-58-27.translation: 'From whom will I now hear, in the last part of the night, the sweet, heart-touching recitation of scripture?'
ramayana-2-58-27.meaning: He will miss his son's voice at study.
ramayana-2-58-27.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-58-28.translation: 'Who, after bathing, performing the twilight worship and offering to the fire, will sit by me and comfort me, tormented by grief and fear for my son?'
ramayana-2-58-28.meaning: He has lost his companion in daily worship.
ramayana-2-58-28.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-58-29.translation: 'Who will bring roots, bulbs and fruit and feed me like a dear guest, helpless, without support and without a leader?'
ramayana-2-58-29.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-58-30.translation: 'Son, how will I support your blind, aged mother, an ascetic, miserable and longing for her son?'
ramayana-2-58-30.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-58-31.translation: 'Stay, son, do not go toward Yama's house. Tomorrow you will go with me and your mother.'
ramayana-2-58-31.meaning: He begs his son to wait for them.
ramayana-2-58-31.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-58-32.translation: 'We two, stricken with grief, helpless and wretched in the forest, will soon go to Yama's realm without you.'
ramayana-2-58-32.meaning: The parents know they will not survive long.
ramayana-2-58-32.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-58-33.translation: 'Then, seeing Vaivasvata, I will say to him: may the king of dharma forgive me, and may this son support his parents.'
ramayana-2-58-33.meaning: Even in death he wants to stay with his son.
ramayana-2-58-33.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-58-34.translation: 'Son, since you are sinless and were killed by one who did a sinful deed, by that truth go quickly to the worlds of those who fight with weapons.'
ramayana-2-58-34.meaning: He blesses his innocent son with a noble afterlife.
ramayana-2-58-34.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-58-35.translation: 'Son, go to that highest state that heroes reach who never turn back in battle and die facing the enemy.'
ramayana-2-58-35.meaning: He wishes his son the reward of the bravest.
ramayana-2-58-35.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-58-36.translation: 'Little son, go to the state reached by Sagara, Shaibya, Dilipa, Janamejaya, Nahusha and Dhundhumara.'
ramayana-2-58-36.meaning: He names great kings of old as models.
ramayana-2-58-36.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-58-37.translation: '...the state of all good people, of those who study and do austerities, of the giver of land, of one who keeps the sacred fire, and of one faithful to a single wife...'
ramayana-2-58-37.meaning: He lists the virtues that lead to heaven.
ramayana-2-58-37.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-58-38.translation: '...the state of givers of a thousand cows, of those who serve their teachers, of those who give up the body; go to that state, little son. No one born in this family goes to an unhappy end.'
ramayana-2-58-38.meaning: He trusts his son's good life will bring him peace.
ramayana-2-58-38.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-58-39.translation: So he lamented there pitifully again and again. Then he began, with his wife, to offer water for him.
ramayana-2-58-39.meaning: They perform the funeral water offering.
ramayana-2-58-39.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-58-40.translation: Then the sage's son, in a divine form gained by his own deeds, comforted his parents for a moment and spoke.
ramayana-2-58-40.meaning: The son appears in heavenly form.
ramayana-2-58-40.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-58-41.translation: 'I have reached a great place through serving you both. You too will soon come to me.'
ramayana-2-58-41.meaning: Serving his parents earned him a high place.
ramayana-2-58-41.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-58-42.translation: Having said this, the self-controlled sage's son quickly rose to heaven in a beautiful divine chariot.
ramayana-2-58-42.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-58-43.translation: The ascetic, with his wife, having quickly made the water offering, spoke to me, the powerful one, as I stood with folded hands.
ramayana-2-58-43.meaning: The father now speaks to Dasharatha.
ramayana-2-58-43.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-58-44.translation: 'Kill me today, king; I have no fear of death, since with one arrow you have made me, who had one son, sonless.'
ramayana-2-58-44.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-58-45.translation: 'Because you killed my pure son through ignorance, I will lay on you a curse of very painful and terrible sorrow.'
ramayana-2-58-45.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-58-46.translation: 'Just as I now feel this pain born of losing my son, so, king, you too will die of grief for a son.'
ramayana-2-58-46.meaning: The curse: Dasharatha will die grieving for a son.
ramayana-2-58-46.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-58-47.translation: Good lady, the words of that noble one have now come true for me, since today I will give up my life from grief for my son.
ramayana-2-58-47.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-58-48.translation: If Rama touched me even once today or held me, that would not match what I have done to Raghava, O queen.
ramayana-2-58-48.meaning: He knows he does not deserve Rama's tenderness.
ramayana-2-58-48.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-58-49.translation: I cannot see you with my eyes, my memory is fading. Kausalya, Yama's messengers are hurrying me.
ramayana-2-58-49.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-58-50.translation: What could be more painful than this, that at the end of my life I cannot see Rama, who knows dharma and is true in valour?
ramayana-2-58-50.meaning: His greatest pain is dying without seeing Rama.
ramayana-2-58-50.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-58-51.translation: They are not men but gods who will see Rama's face with its lovely bright earrings again in the fifteenth year.
ramayana-2-58-51.meaning: Those who see Rama return will be blessed.
ramayana-2-58-51.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-58-52.translation: Fortunate are those who will see Rama's face, with lotus-petal eyes, fine brows, fine teeth and lovely nose, shining like the moon.
ramayana-2-58-52.meaning: He imagines the lucky ones who will see Rama.
ramayana-2-58-52.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-58-53.translation: Fortunate are those who will see my lord's fragrant face, like the autumn moon and a blooming lotus.
ramayana-2-58-53.meaning: He calls Rama his lord in his love.
ramayana-2-58-53.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-58-54.translation: Happy are those who will see Rama, his forest exile over, come back to Ayodhya, like the planet Venus back on its course.
ramayana-2-58-54.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-58-55.translation: This grief, born of my own deeds, wears me down, helpless and senseless, as a river's current wears away its bank.
ramayana-2-58-55.meaning: His own actions have brought this ruin.
ramayana-2-58-55.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-58-56.translation: 'Alas Raghava, mighty-armed! Alas, destroyer of my troubles!' So grieving, King Dasharatha came to the end of his life.
ramayana-2-58-56.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-58-57.translation: Speaking so pitifully, distressed by the exile of his beloved son, the noble-looking king, crushed by deep grief, gave up his life after midnight.
ramayana-2-58-57.meaning: The king dies of grief, as the curse foretold.
ramayana-2-58-57.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 58: Dasharatha carries water to the blind old couple and confesses. The grieving father, sparing him because the killing was not deliberate, curses him to die of grief for a son. The son rises to heaven. Having finished the story, Dasharatha, longing for Rama, dies at midnight.

ramayana-2-59-1.translation: When the night had passed, early the next morning, the bards came to attend at the king's palace.
ramayana-2-59-1.meaning: Morning routines begin as if all is normal.
ramayana-2-59-1.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 59: At dawn the palace attendants come to wake the king as usual and find him dead. The queens and the household break into lamentation.

ramayana-2-59-2.translation: Then the attendants, pure in conduct and skilled in service, mostly women and eunuchs, came as before.
ramayana-2-59-2.meaning: The household staff arrive to serve the king.
ramayana-2-59-2.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 59: At dawn the palace attendants come to wake the king as usual and find him dead. The queens and the household break into lamentation.

ramayana-2-59-3.translation: Those who knew the rites of bathing brought water mixed with yellow sandal in golden pots, at the right time and in the proper way.
ramayana-2-59-3.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 59: At dawn the palace attendants come to wake the king as usual and find him dead. The queens and the household break into lamentation.

ramayana-2-59-4.translation: Other women, many of them young girls, brought auspicious things to touch, food and utensils.
ramayana-2-59-4.meaning: Everything is readied for the king's morning.
ramayana-2-59-4.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 59: At dawn the palace attendants come to wake the king as usual and find him dead. The queens and the household break into lamentation.

ramayana-2-59-5.translation: Then the women closest to the king's bed came together and tried to wake their lord.
ramayana-2-59-5.meaning: They try to wake the king.
ramayana-2-59-5.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 59: At dawn the palace attendants come to wake the king as usual and find him dead. The queens and the household break into lamentation.

ramayana-2-59-6.translation: Trembling and fearing for the king's life, they shook like grass tips against a stream.
ramayana-2-59-6.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 59: At dawn the palace attendants come to wake the king as usual and find him dead. The queens and the household break into lamentation.

ramayana-2-59-7.translation: Then, seeing the trembling women and the king, their fear that something terrible had happened became certain.
ramayana-2-59-7.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 59: At dawn the palace attendants come to wake the king as usual and find him dead. The queens and the household break into lamentation.

ramayana-2-59-8.translation: Then the fine ladies cried out aloud in misery, like female elephants in the forest whose herd leader has fallen.
ramayana-2-59-8.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 59: At dawn the palace attendants come to wake the king as usual and find him dead. The queens and the household break into lamentation.

ramayana-2-59-9.translation: At the sound of their wailing, Kausalya and Sumitra woke suddenly from sleep.
ramayana-2-59-9.meaning: The queens wake to the cries.
ramayana-2-59-9.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 59: At dawn the palace attendants come to wake the king as usual and find him dead. The queens and the household break into lamentation.

ramayana-2-59-10.translation: Kausalya and Sumitra, seeing and touching the king, cried 'Alas, my lord!' and fell to the ground.
ramayana-2-59-10.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 59: At dawn the palace attendants come to wake the king as usual and find him dead. The queens and the household break into lamentation.

ramayana-2-59-11.translation: The daughter of the Kosala king, rolling on the ground, covered in dust, lost her lustre like a star fallen from the sky.
ramayana-2-59-11.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 59: At dawn the palace attendants come to wake the king as usual and find him dead. The queens and the household break into lamentation.

ramayana-2-59-12.translation: ...full of terrified, bewildered and anxious people, everywhere loud lamentation, kinsmen tormented with grief...
ramayana-2-59-12.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 59: At dawn the palace attendants come to wake the king as usual and find him dead. The queens and the household break into lamentation.

ramayana-2-59-13.translation: ...all joy suddenly gone, a sight of misery and confusion: so became the palace of the king who had met his end.
ramayana-2-59-13.meaning: Joy has vanished from the palace.
ramayana-2-59-13.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 59: At dawn the palace attendants come to wake the king as usual and find him dead. The queens and the household break into lamentation.

ramayana-2-59-14.translation: Knowing that the famous bull among kings had passed away, his wives gathered round him, weeping bitterly and pitifully, and holding his arms lamented like orphans.
ramayana-2-59-14.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 59: At dawn the palace attendants come to wake the king as usual and find him dead. The queens and the household break into lamentation.

ramayana-2-60-1.translation: Seeing the king gone to heaven, like a fire gone out, like an ocean without water, like a sun without light...
ramayana-2-60-1.meaning: The king's death is described through images of lost power.
ramayana-2-60-1.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 60: Kausalya grieves over the dead king and turns on Kaikeyi. The ministers preserve the king's body in oil until Bharata can return.

ramayana-2-60-2.translation: ...Kausalya, her eyes full of tears, worn down by grief in many ways, took the king's head in her lap and spoke to Kaikeyi.
ramayana-2-60-2.meaning: Kausalya turns to Kaikeyi in her sorrow.
ramayana-2-60-2.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 60: Kausalya grieves over the dead king and turns on Kaikeyi. The ministers preserve the king's body in oil until Bharata can return.

ramayana-2-60-3.translation: Have your wish, Kaikeyi. Enjoy the kingdom without a rival, having cast off the king, single-minded, cruel woman of wicked conduct.
ramayana-2-60-3.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 60: Kausalya, holding the dead king's head, rebukes Kaikeyi. The ministers place the king's body in a vessel of oil to preserve it until a son can perform the last rites, and Ayodhya sinks into mourning.

ramayana-2-60-4.translation: Rama has left me and gone, and my husband has gone to heaven. Like a traveller who has lost her caravan on a bad road, I cannot bear to live.
ramayana-2-60-4.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 60: Kausalya, holding the dead king's head, rebukes Kaikeyi. The ministers place the king's body in a vessel of oil to preserve it until a son can perform the last rites, and Ayodhya sinks into mourning.

ramayana-2-60-5.translation: What woman, having abandoned her husband, her god, would wish to live elsewhere, except Kaikeyi who has abandoned dharma?
ramayana-2-60-5.meaning: She accuses Kaikeyi of betraying her duty.
ramayana-2-60-5.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 60: Kausalya, holding the dead king's head, rebukes Kaikeyi. The ministers place the king's body in a vessel of oil to preserve it until a son can perform the last rites, and Ayodhya sinks into mourning.

ramayana-2-60-6.translation: A greedy person does not see the faults, like one eating poisonous fruit. Because of the hunchbacked woman, Kaikeyi has destroyed the family of the Raghavas.
ramayana-2-60-6.meaning: Greed blinds people to the harm they cause.
ramayana-2-60-6.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 60: Kausalya, holding the dead king's head, rebukes Kaikeyi. The ministers place the king's body in a vessel of oil to preserve it until a son can perform the last rites, and Ayodhya sinks into mourning. The reference to Manthara's body is a label of the time; the point is her influence, not her appearance.

ramayana-2-60-7.translation: When Janaka hears that Rama and his wife were exiled by the king under an improper command, he will grieve as I do.
ramayana-2-60-7.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 60: Kausalya, holding the dead king's head, rebukes Kaikeyi. The ministers place the king's body in a vessel of oil to preserve it until a son can perform the last rites, and Ayodhya sinks into mourning.

ramayana-2-60-8.translation: Lotus-eyed Rama has gone from here as if to his death. And Sita, the poor daughter of the king of Videha, who never knew sorrow, will be distressed by hardship in the forest.
ramayana-2-60-8.meaning: Kausalya fears for Rama and Sita.
ramayana-2-60-8.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 60: Kausalya, holding the dead king's head, rebukes Kaikeyi. The ministers place the king's body in a vessel of oil to preserve it until a son can perform the last rites, and Ayodhya sinks into mourning.

ramayana-2-60-9.translation: Hearing at night the terrible cries of beasts and birds, she will surely be frightened and cling to Raghava.
ramayana-2-60-9.meaning: She imagines Sita frightened in the night.
ramayana-2-60-9.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 60: Kausalya, holding the dead king's head, rebukes Kaikeyi. The ministers place the king's body in a vessel of oil to preserve it until a son can perform the last rites, and Ayodhya sinks into mourning.

ramayana-2-60-10.translation: Old, with only one child, thinking constantly of Vaidehi, he too, overcome by grief, will surely give up his life.
ramayana-2-60-10.meaning: She fears Janaka too may die of sorrow.
ramayana-2-60-10.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 60: Kausalya, holding the dead king's head, rebukes Kaikeyi. The ministers place the king's body in a vessel of oil to preserve it until a son can perform the last rites, and Ayodhya sinks into mourning.

ramayana-2-60-11.translation: Then the attendants embraced the weeping, wretched Kausalya, deeply stricken with sorrow, and led her away.
ramayana-2-60-11.meaning: The household gently leads Kausalya away.
ramayana-2-60-11.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 60: Kausalya, holding the dead king's head, rebukes Kaikeyi. The ministers place the king's body in a vessel of oil to preserve it until a son can perform the last rites, and Ayodhya sinks into mourning.

ramayana-2-60-12.translation: Then the ministers laid the lord of the earth in a vessel of oil and, as instructed, did all the necessary things for the king.
ramayana-2-60-12.meaning: The body is preserved in oil.
ramayana-2-60-12.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 60: Kausalya, holding the dead king's head, rebukes Kaikeyi. The ministers place the king's body in a vessel of oil to preserve it until a son can perform the last rites, and Ayodhya sinks into mourning.

ramayana-2-60-13.translation: The all-knowing ministers did not wish to perform the king's funeral without a son, so they kept the king's body safe.
ramayana-2-60-13.meaning: Last rites must wait for a son.
ramayana-2-60-13.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 60: Kausalya, holding the dead king's head, rebukes Kaikeyi. The ministers place the king's body in a vessel of oil to preserve it until a son can perform the last rites, and Ayodhya sinks into mourning.

ramayana-2-60-14.translation: When the women learned that the king, laid in the oil vessel by the ministers, was truly dead, they lamented.
ramayana-2-60-14.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 60: Kausalya, holding the dead king's head, rebukes Kaikeyi. The ministers place the king's body in a vessel of oil to preserve it until a son can perform the last rites, and Ayodhya sinks into mourning.

ramayana-2-60-15.translation: Raising their arms, wretched, faces streaming with tears, burning with grief, they wept and lamented pitifully.
ramayana-2-60-15.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 60: Kausalya, holding the dead king's head, rebukes Kaikeyi. The ministers place the king's body in a vessel of oil to preserve it until a son can perform the last rites, and Ayodhya sinks into mourning.

ramayana-2-60-16.translation: Without its great-souled king, the city of Ayodhya did not shine, like a night without stars or a woman without her husband.
ramayana-2-60-16.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 60: Kausalya, holding the dead king's head, rebukes Kaikeyi. The ministers place the king's body in a vessel of oil to preserve it until a son can perform the last rites, and Ayodhya sinks into mourning.

ramayana-2-60-17.translation: With people choked by tears, the noble women crying 'Alas!', its squares and houses empty, it did not shine as before.
ramayana-2-60-17.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 60: Kausalya, holding the dead king's head, rebukes Kaikeyi. The ministers place the king's body in a vessel of oil to preserve it until a son can perform the last rites, and Ayodhya sinks into mourning.

ramayana-2-60-18.translation: Bereft of the great one, the city looked like the sky without the sun, or a night with its hosts of stars gone, its roads and squares filled with tear-choked people.
ramayana-2-60-18.meaning: Without the king, the city seems dark.
ramayana-2-60-18.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 60: Kausalya, holding the dead king's head, rebukes Kaikeyi. The ministers place the king's body in a vessel of oil to preserve it until a son can perform the last rites, and Ayodhya sinks into mourning.

ramayana-2-60-19.translation: Then in the city, at the king's death, men and women gathered in groups condemning Bharata's mother; they were in distress and found no peace.
ramayana-2-60-19.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 60: Kausalya, holding the dead king's head, rebukes Kaikeyi. The ministers place the king's body in a vessel of oil to preserve it until a son can perform the last rites, and Ayodhya sinks into mourning.

ramayana-2-61-1.translation: When the night had passed and the sun rose, the twice-born who were the king-makers gathered and went to the assembly hall.
ramayana-2-61-1.meaning: The leaders meet to decide what to do.
ramayana-2-61-1.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 61: The next morning the sages and ministers gather. They describe, verse by verse, the chaos that befalls a land without a ruler, and urge Vasishtha to install a prince as king at once. The passage is a classic Indian reflection on why order and just government matter.

ramayana-2-61-2.translation: Markandeya, Maudgalya, Vamadeva, Kashyapa, Katyayana, Gautama and the famous Jabali...
ramayana-2-61-2.meaning: The great sages of the court are named.
ramayana-2-61-2.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 61: The next morning the sages and ministers gather. They describe, verse by verse, the chaos that befalls a land without a ruler, and urge Vasishtha to install a prince as king at once. The passage is a classic Indian reflection on why order and just government matter.

ramayana-2-61-3.translation: These Brahmins, with the ministers, each spoke out, facing Vasishtha, the best of royal priests.
ramayana-2-61-3.meaning: They address the royal priest Vasishtha.
ramayana-2-61-3.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 61: The next morning the sages and ministers gather. They describe, verse by verse, the chaos that befalls a land without a ruler, and urge Vasishtha to install a prince as king at once. The passage is a classic Indian reflection on why order and just government matter.

ramayana-2-61-4.translation: This night has passed in sorrow, like a hundred years for us, now that the king has died of grief for his son.
ramayana-2-61-4.meaning: The night of mourning felt endless.
ramayana-2-61-4.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 61: The next morning the sages and ministers gather. They describe, verse by verse, the chaos that befalls a land without a ruler, and urge Vasishtha to install a prince as king at once. The passage is a classic Indian reflection on why order and just government matter.

ramayana-2-61-5.translation: The great king has gone to heaven, Rama has gone to the forest, and splendid Lakshmana has gone with him.
ramayana-2-61-5.meaning: The kingdom has lost its leaders.
ramayana-2-61-5.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 61: The next morning the sages and ministers gather. They describe, verse by verse, the chaos that befalls a land without a ruler, and urge Vasishtha to install a prince as king at once. The passage is a classic Indian reflection on why order and just government matter.

ramayana-2-61-6.translation: Both Bharata and Shatrughna, scorchers of foes, are in Kekaya, in the lovely city of Rajagriha, in their grandfather's home.
ramayana-2-61-6.meaning: The remaining princes are far away.
ramayana-2-61-6.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 61: The next morning the sages and ministers gather. They describe, verse by verse, the chaos that befalls a land without a ruler, and urge Vasishtha to install a prince as king at once. The passage is a classic Indian reflection on why order and just government matter.

ramayana-2-61-7.translation: Let some Ikshvaku prince be made king here this very day, so that our kingless land does not fall to ruin.
ramayana-2-61-7.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 61: The next morning the sages and ministers gather. They describe, verse by verse, the chaos that befalls a land without a ruler, and urge Vasishtha to install a prince as king at once. The passage is a classic Indian reflection on why order and just government matter.

ramayana-2-61-8.translation: In a kingless land the thundering rain-cloud, garlanded with lightning, does not pour heavenly water on the earth.
ramayana-2-61-8.meaning: Without order, even nature seems to fail.
ramayana-2-61-8.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 61: The next morning the sages and ministers gather. They describe, verse by verse, the chaos that befalls a land without a ruler, and urge Vasishtha to install a prince as king at once. The passage is a classic Indian reflection on why order and just government matter.

ramayana-2-61-9.translation: In a kingless land no handful of seed is sown. In a kingless land a son does not obey his father, nor a wife her husband.
ramayana-2-61-9.meaning: Disorder spreads from public life into families.
ramayana-2-61-9.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 61: The next morning the sages and ministers gather. They describe, verse by verse, the chaos that befalls a land without a ruler, and urge Vasishtha to install a prince as king at once. The passage is a classic Indian reflection on why order and just government matter.

ramayana-2-61-10.translation: In a kingless land there is no wealth, no wife is safe; and here is a further great danger: how can there be truth in a kingless land?
ramayana-2-61-10.meaning: Without just rule, property, safety and honesty collapse.
ramayana-2-61-10.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 61: The next morning the sages and ministers gather. They describe, verse by verse, the chaos that befalls a land without a ruler, and urge Vasishtha to install a prince as king at once. The passage is a classic Indian reflection on why order and just government matter.

ramayana-2-61-11.translation: In a kingless land people do not build assembly halls, lovely gardens or holy shrines with joy.
ramayana-2-61-11.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 61: The next morning the sages and ministers gather. They describe, verse by verse, the chaos that befalls a land without a ruler, and urge Vasishtha to install a prince as king at once. The passage is a classic Indian reflection on why order and just government matter.

ramayana-2-61-12.translation: In a kingless land the twice-born devoted to sacrifice, the self-controlled Brahmins of strict vows, do not hold long sacrificial sessions.
ramayana-2-61-12.meaning: Spiritual life too needs a stable society.
ramayana-2-61-12.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 61: The next morning the sages and ministers gather. They describe, verse by verse, the chaos that befalls a land without a ruler, and urge Vasishtha to install a prince as king at once. The passage is a classic Indian reflection on why order and just government matter.

ramayana-2-61-13.translation: In a kingless land there are no crowds of actors and dancers, and festivals and gatherings that enrich the realm do not flourish.
ramayana-2-61-13.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 61: The next morning the sages and ministers gather. They describe, verse by verse, the chaos that befalls a land without a ruler, and urge Vasishtha to install a prince as king at once. The passage is a classic Indian reflection on why order and just government matter.

ramayana-2-61-14.translation: In a kingless land successful litigants find no joy, and storytellers are not delighted by those who love stories.
ramayana-2-61-14.meaning: Without order, justice and simple pleasures fail.
ramayana-2-61-14.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 61: The next morning the sages and ministers gather. They describe, verse by verse, the chaos that befalls a land without a ruler, and urge Vasishtha to install a prince as king at once. The passage is a classic Indian reflection on why order and just government matter.

ramayana-2-61-15.translation: In a kingless land men do not ride out to the woods on swift vehicles with their women for pleasure.
ramayana-2-61-15.meaning: People cannot travel freely for leisure.
ramayana-2-61-15.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 61: The next morning the sages and ministers gather. They describe, verse by verse, the chaos that befalls a land without a ruler, and urge Vasishtha to install a prince as king at once. The passage is a classic Indian reflection on why order and just government matter.

ramayana-2-61-16.translation: In a kingless land the wealthy are not protected, and farmers and herdsmen do not sleep with their doors open.
ramayana-2-61-16.meaning: Safety at home depends on good governance.
ramayana-2-61-16.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 61: The next morning the sages and ministers gather. They describe, verse by verse, the chaos that befalls a land without a ruler, and urge Vasishtha to install a prince as king at once. The passage is a classic Indian reflection on why order and just government matter.

ramayana-2-61-17.translation: In a kingless land merchants who travel far, carrying many goods, do not take the road in safety.
ramayana-2-61-17.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 61: The next morning the sages and ministers gather. They describe, verse by verse, the chaos that befalls a land without a ruler, and urge Vasishtha to install a prince as king at once. The passage is a classic Indian reflection on why order and just government matter.

ramayana-2-61-18.translation: In a kingless land the self-controlled sage who wanders alone, contemplating the self by the self and making his home wherever evening finds him, does not roam.
ramayana-2-61-18.meaning: Even the wandering seeker needs a peaceful society.
ramayana-2-61-18.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 61: The next morning the sages and ministers gather. They describe, verse by verse, the chaos that befalls a land without a ruler, and urge Vasishtha to install a prince as king at once. The passage is a classic Indian reflection on why order and just government matter.

ramayana-2-61-19.translation: In a kingless land welfare and security do not continue, and without a king an army cannot withstand enemies in battle.
ramayana-2-61-19.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 61: The next morning the sages and ministers gather. They describe, verse by verse, the chaos that befalls a land without a ruler, and urge Vasishtha to install a prince as king at once. The passage is a classic Indian reflection on why order and just government matter.

ramayana-2-61-20.translation: Like rivers without water, like a forest without grass, like cows without a herdsman, so is a kingdom without a king.
ramayana-2-61-20.meaning: A society without good leadership is barren and vulnerable.
ramayana-2-61-20.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 61: The next morning the sages and ministers gather. They describe, verse by verse, the chaos that befalls a land without a ruler, and urge Vasishtha to install a prince as king at once. The passage is a classic Indian reflection on why order and just government matter.

ramayana-2-61-21.translation: In a kingless land nothing belongs to anyone. People always devour each other like fish.
ramayana-2-61-21.meaning: Without law, the strong prey on the weak ('the law of the fishes').
ramayana-2-61-21.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 61: The next morning the sages and ministers gather. They describe, verse by verse, the chaos that befalls a land without a ruler, and urge Vasishtha to install a prince as king at once. The passage is a classic Indian reflection on why order and just government matter.

ramayana-2-61-22.translation: Even those who break all bounds, unbelievers whose doubts have been cut off, come to good behaviour when restrained by the king's rod of justice.
ramayana-2-61-22.meaning: Fair laws keep even the unruly in check.
ramayana-2-61-22.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 61: The next morning the sages and ministers gather. They describe, verse by verse, the chaos that befalls a land without a ruler, and urge Vasishtha to install a prince as king at once. The passage is a classic Indian reflection on why order and just government matter.

ramayana-2-61-23.translation: Ah, if there were no king in the world to separate good from bad, all would be like darkness and nothing would be clear.
ramayana-2-61-23.meaning: Justice is what lets us tell right from wrong in public life.
ramayana-2-61-23.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 61: The next morning the sages and ministers gather. They describe, verse by verse, the chaos that befalls a land without a ruler, and urge Vasishtha to install a prince as king at once. The passage is a classic Indian reflection on why order and just government matter.

ramayana-2-61-24.translation: Even while the great king lived, we all never overstepped your word, just as the ocean does not pass its shore.
ramayana-2-61-24.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 61: The next morning the sages and ministers gather. They describe, verse by verse, the chaos that befalls a land without a ruler, and urge Vasishtha to install a prince as king at once. The passage is a classic Indian reflection on why order and just government matter.

ramayana-2-61-25.translation: Best of Brahmins, seeing how the kingdom without a king has become like a wilderness, you yourself consecrate as king here a generous Ikshvaku prince.
ramayana-2-61-25.meaning: They ask Vasishtha to choose and crown a prince.
ramayana-2-61-25.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 61: The next morning the sages and ministers gather. They describe, verse by verse, the chaos that befalls a land without a ruler, and urge Vasishtha to install a prince as king at once. The passage is a classic Indian reflection on why order and just government matter.

ramayana-2-62-1.translation: Hearing their words, Vasishtha replied to all the friends, ministers and Brahmins.
ramayana-2-62-1.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 62: Vasishtha sends swift messengers to fetch Bharata and Shatrughna from their grandfather's city Rajagriha in Kekaya, telling them to keep the king's death and Rama's exile secret. The route of their journey is described.

ramayana-2-62-2.translation: Since Bharata lives happily in his uncle's house in the city of Rajagriha, together with his brother Shatrughna...
ramayana-2-62-2.meaning: He points out that Bharata is the heir.
ramayana-2-62-2.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 62: Vasishtha sends swift messengers to fetch Bharata and Shatrughna from their grandfather's city Rajagriha in Kekaya, telling them to keep the king's death and Rama's exile secret. The route of their journey is described.

ramayana-2-62-3.translation: ...let swift messengers go quickly on fast horses to bring the two heroic brothers. What else should we consider?
ramayana-2-62-3.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 62: Vasishtha sends swift messengers to fetch Bharata and Shatrughna from their grandfather's city Rajagriha in Kekaya, telling them to keep the king's death and Rama's exile secret. The route of their journey is described.

ramayana-2-62-4.translation: 'Let them go,' they all said to Vasishtha. Hearing their words, Vasishtha spoke.
ramayana-2-62-4.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 62: Vasishtha sends swift messengers to fetch Bharata and Shatrughna from their grandfather's city Rajagriha in Kekaya, telling them to keep the king's death and Rama's exile secret. The route of their journey is described.

ramayana-2-62-5.translation: Come, Siddhartha, Vijaya, Jayanta, Ashoka and Nandana. Listen to what must be done; I tell all of you.
ramayana-2-62-5.meaning: He calls the messengers by name.
ramayana-2-62-5.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 62: Vasishtha sends swift messengers to fetch Bharata and Shatrughna from their grandfather's city Rajagriha in Kekaya, telling them to keep the king's death and Rama's exile secret. The route of their journey is described.

ramayana-2-62-6.translation: Go quickly to the city of Rajagriha on swift horses, put aside your grief, and say this to Bharata at my command.
ramayana-2-62-6.meaning: They are to hide their sorrow.
ramayana-2-62-6.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 62: Vasishtha sends swift messengers to fetch Bharata and Shatrughna from their grandfather's city Rajagriha in Kekaya, telling them to keep the king's death and Rama's exile secret. The route of their journey is described.

ramayana-2-62-7.translation: 'The royal priest and all the ministers wish you well. Set out quickly; there is urgent business for you.'
ramayana-2-62-7.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 62: Vasishtha sends swift messengers to fetch Bharata and Shatrughna from their grandfather's city Rajagriha in Kekaya, telling them to keep the king's death and Rama's exile secret. The route of their journey is described.

ramayana-2-62-8.translation: Do not tell him that Rama has been exiled or that his father is dead, this ruin of the Raghavas.
ramayana-2-62-8.meaning: The bad news is to be held back until Bharata arrives.
ramayana-2-62-8.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 62: Vasishtha sends swift messengers to fetch Bharata and Shatrughna from their grandfather's city Rajagriha in Kekaya, telling them to keep the king's death and Rama's exile secret. The route of their journey is described.

ramayana-2-62-9.translation: Take silk garments and fine ornaments quickly for the king and for Bharata, and go.' Permitted by Vasishtha, the messengers left in haste.
ramayana-2-62-9.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 62: Vasishtha sends swift messengers to fetch Bharata and Shatrughna from their grandfather's city Rajagriha in Kekaya, telling them to keep the king's death and Rama's exile secret. The route of their journey is described.

ramayana-2-62-10.translation: They crossed the Ganga at Hastinapura and went west, reaching the Panchala country and passing through the middle of Kurujangala.
ramayana-2-62-10.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 62: Vasishtha sends swift messengers to fetch Bharata and Shatrughna from their grandfather's city Rajagriha in Kekaya, telling them to keep the king's death and Rama's exile secret. The route of their journey is described.

ramayana-2-62-11.translation: They swiftly passed the Sharadanda river, with its clear water, divine and frequented by many birds, crowded with people.
ramayana-2-62-11.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 62: Vasishtha sends swift messengers to fetch Bharata and Shatrughna from their grandfather's city Rajagriha in Kekaya, telling them to keep the king's death and Rama's exile secret. The route of their journey is described.

ramayana-2-62-12.translation: Reaching the divine tree on the riverbank called Satyopayachana, they approached and saluted it, and entered the city of Kulinga.
ramayana-2-62-12.meaning: They honour a sacred tree on the way.
ramayana-2-62-12.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 62: Vasishtha sends swift messengers to fetch Bharata and Shatrughna from their grandfather's city Rajagriha in Kekaya, telling them to keep the king's death and Rama's exile secret. The route of their journey is described.

ramayana-2-62-13.translation: Then reaching Abhikala, they went through the Bahlika country and Mount Sudaman, looking at Vishnu's footprint, the Vipasha river and the Shalmali.
ramayana-2-62-13.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 62: Vasishtha sends swift messengers to fetch Bharata and Shatrughna from their grandfather's city Rajagriha in Kekaya, telling them to keep the king's death and Rama's exile secret. The route of their journey is described.

ramayana-2-62-14.translation: Their horses tired, the messengers reached the fine city of Girivraja quickly and directly by a long, good road.
ramayana-2-62-14.meaning: They arrive at the capital of Kekaya.
ramayana-2-62-14.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 62: Vasishtha sends swift messengers to fetch Bharata and Shatrughna from their grandfather's city Rajagriha in Kekaya, telling them to keep the king's death and Rama's exile secret. The route of their journey is described.

ramayana-2-62-15.translation: To please their master, to protect the family and secure the royal line, the messengers, never slackening, hurried and reached that city at night.
ramayana-2-62-15.meaning: They travel with dedication to duty.
ramayana-2-62-15.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 62: Vasishtha sends swift messengers to fetch Bharata and Shatrughna from their grandfather's city Rajagriha in Kekaya, telling them to keep the king's death and Rama's exile secret. The route of their journey is described.

ramayana-2-63-1.translation: On the very night the messengers entered the city, Bharata had an unpleasant dream.
ramayana-2-63-1.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 63: On the night the messengers arrive, Bharata has a disturbing dream full of omens of his father's death. His friends try to cheer him, but he remains troubled.

ramayana-2-63-2.translation: When that night ended, having seen that unpleasant dream, the son of the king of kings was deeply troubled.
ramayana-2-63-2.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 63: On the night the messengers arrive, Bharata has a disturbing dream full of omens of his father's death. His friends try to cheer him, but he remains troubled.

ramayana-2-63-3.translation: Seeing him troubled, his friends, pleasant in speech, told stories in the hall to ease his distress.
ramayana-2-63-3.meaning: His friends try to lift his mood.
ramayana-2-63-3.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 63: On the night the messengers arrive, Bharata has a disturbing dream full of omens of his father's death. His friends try to cheer him, but he remains troubled.

ramayana-2-63-4.translation: Some played calming music, others had dancers perform, others told plays and many kinds of jokes.
ramayana-2-63-4.meaning: They try music, dance and humour.
ramayana-2-63-4.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 63: On the night the messengers arrive, Bharata has a disturbing dream full of omens of his father's death. His friends try to cheer him, but he remains troubled.

ramayana-2-63-5.translation: But great-souled Bharata, of the Raghu line, did not cheer up with those kind friends who joked in company.
ramayana-2-63-5.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 63: On the night the messengers arrive, Bharata has a disturbing dream full of omens of his father's death. His friends try to cheer him, but he remains troubled.

ramayana-2-63-6.translation: His dear friend, sitting among the companions, asked Bharata, 'Why, friend, do you not enjoy yourself?'
ramayana-2-63-6.meaning: A friend asks what is wrong.
ramayana-2-63-6.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 63: On the night the messengers arrive, Bharata has a disturbing dream full of omens of his father's death. His friends try to cheer him, but he remains troubled.

ramayana-2-63-7.translation: Bharata replied to his friend: 'Listen to why this gloom has come upon me.'
ramayana-2-63-7.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 63: On the night the messengers arrive, Bharata has a disturbing dream full of omens of his father's death. His friends try to cheer him, but he remains troubled.

ramayana-2-63-8.translation: In a dream I saw my father, dirty, his hair loose, falling from a mountain peak into a foul pool of cow dung.
ramayana-2-63-8.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 63: On the night the messengers arrive, Bharata has a disturbing dream full of omens of his father's death. His friends try to cheer him, but he remains troubled.

ramayana-2-63-9.translation: I saw him floating in that pool of dung, drinking oil from his cupped hands and laughing again and again.
ramayana-2-63-9.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 63: On the night the messengers arrive, Bharata has a disturbing dream full of omens of his father's death. His friends try to cheer him, but he remains troubled.

ramayana-2-63-10.translation: Then eating rice with sesame, again and again head down, his whole body smeared with oil, he plunged into oil.
ramayana-2-63-10.meaning: Oil and sesame were traditionally linked with death rites.
ramayana-2-63-10.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 63: On the night the messengers arrive, Bharata has a disturbing dream full of omens of his father's death. His friends try to cheer him, but he remains troubled.

ramayana-2-63-11.translation: In the dream I also saw the ocean dried up, the moon fallen to the earth, and the blazing fire suddenly gone out.
ramayana-2-63-11.meaning: Images of the natural order collapsing.
ramayana-2-63-11.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 63: On the night the messengers arrive, Bharata has a disturbing dream full of omens of his father's death. His friends try to cheer him, but he remains troubled.

ramayana-2-63-12.translation: I see the earth split open, many kinds of trees withered, and mountains shattered and smoking.
ramayana-2-63-12.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 63: On the night the messengers arrive, Bharata has a disturbing dream full of omens of his father's death. His friends try to cheer him, but he remains troubled.

ramayana-2-63-13.translation: Dark and tawny women laughed at the king as he sat on an iron seat wearing black clothes.
ramayana-2-63-13.meaning: Black clothing and iron were omens of death.
ramayana-2-63-13.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 63: On the night the messengers arrive, Bharata has a disturbing dream full of omens of his father's death. His friends try to cheer him, but he remains troubled.

ramayana-2-63-14.translation: And the righteous king, wearing red garlands and red paste, went off hastily southward in a chariot drawn by donkeys.
ramayana-2-63-14.meaning: Travelling south was associated with the realm of death.
ramayana-2-63-14.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 63: On the night the messengers arrive, Bharata has a disturbing dream full of omens of his father's death. His friends try to cheer him, but he remains troubled.

ramayana-2-63-15.translation: This is what I saw this frightening night. I, Rama, the king or Lakshmana will die.
ramayana-2-63-15.meaning: Bharata fears a death in the family.
ramayana-2-63-15.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 63: On the night the messengers arrive, Bharata has a disturbing dream full of omens of his father's death. His friends try to cheer him, but he remains troubled.

ramayana-2-63-16.translation: A man who in a dream rides a chariot drawn by donkeys soon has the smoke of his pyre seen. This is why I am gloomy and do not respond to you.
ramayana-2-63-16.meaning: He explains the traditional meaning of the omen.
ramayana-2-63-16.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 63: On the night the messengers arrive, Bharata has a disturbing dream full of omens of his father's death. His friends try to cheer him, but he remains troubled.

ramayana-2-63-17.translation: My throat seems dry, my mind is not at ease. I feel as if I loathe myself, yet I see no reason.
ramayana-2-63-17.meaning: He feels a dread he cannot explain.
ramayana-2-63-17.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 63: On the night the messengers arrive, Bharata has a disturbing dream full of omens of his father's death. His friends try to cheer him, but he remains troubled.

ramayana-2-63-18.translation: Hearing this many-sided course of a bad dream, never imagined before, and thinking of the king whose face I cannot picture, a great fear will not leave my heart.
ramayana-2-63-18.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 63: On the night the messengers arrive, Bharata has a disturbing dream full of omens of his father's death. His friends try to cheer him, but he remains troubled.

ramayana-2-64-1.translation: While Bharata was telling his dream, the messengers with their tired horses entered the lovely city of Rajagriha with its impassable moat.
ramayana-2-64-1.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 64: The messengers deliver Vasishtha's summons. Bharata asks after everyone at home, then takes leave of his grandfather, the king of Kekaya, who sends him off with rich gifts.

ramayana-2-64-2.translation: Meeting the king and the prince and being honoured by them, they clasped the king's feet and spoke to Bharata.
ramayana-2-64-2.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 64: The messengers deliver Vasishtha's summons. Bharata asks after everyone at home, then takes leave of his grandfather, the king of Kekaya, who sends him off with rich gifts.

ramayana-2-64-3.translation: 'The royal priest and all the ministers wish you well. Set out quickly; there is urgent business for you.'
ramayana-2-64-3.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 64: The messengers deliver Vasishtha's summons. Bharata asks after everyone at home, then takes leave of his grandfather, the king of Kekaya, who sends him off with rich gifts.

ramayana-2-64-4.translation: 'Here are two hundred million for the king, your uncle, and a full hundred million for you, prince.'
ramayana-2-64-4.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 64: The messengers deliver Vasishtha's summons. Bharata asks after everyone at home, then takes leave of his grandfather, the king of Kekaya, who sends him off with rich gifts.

ramayana-2-64-5.translation: Accepting it all, Bharata, devoted to his friends, honoured the messengers with what they wished and spoke to them.
ramayana-2-64-5.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 64: The messengers deliver Vasishtha's summons. Bharata asks after everyone at home, then takes leave of his grandfather, the king of Kekaya, who sends him off with rich gifts.

ramayana-2-64-6.translation: Is my father, King Dasharatha, well? Is there good health for Rama and for great-souled Lakshmana?
ramayana-2-64-6.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 64: The messengers deliver Vasishtha's summons. Bharata asks after everyone at home, then takes leave of his grandfather, the king of Kekaya, who sends him off with rich gifts.

ramayana-2-64-7.translation: Is noble Kausalya, devoted to dharma, knowing and seeing dharma, the mother of wise Rama, in good health?
ramayana-2-64-7.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 64: The messengers deliver Vasishtha's summons. Bharata asks after everyone at home, then takes leave of his grandfather, the king of Kekaya, who sends him off with rich gifts.

ramayana-2-64-8.translation: Is Sumitra, who knows dharma, the mother of Lakshmana and heroic Shatrughna, the middle queen, well?
ramayana-2-64-8.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 64: The messengers deliver Vasishtha's summons. Bharata asks after everyone at home, then takes leave of his grandfather, the king of Kekaya, who sends him off with rich gifts.

ramayana-2-64-9.translation: And my mother Kaikeyi, always selfish, fierce, quick to anger, proud of her cleverness, is she well? What did she say?
ramayana-2-64-9.meaning: Bharata is frank about his mother's faults.
ramayana-2-64-9.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 64: The messengers deliver Vasishtha's summons. Bharata asks after everyone at home, then takes leave of his grandfather, the king of Kekaya, who sends him off with rich gifts.

ramayana-2-64-10.translation: Addressed so by great-souled Bharata, the messengers then said politely to him: 'Those whose welfare you wish for are well, tiger among men.'
ramayana-2-64-10.meaning: The messengers give a careful, evasive answer.
ramayana-2-64-10.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 64: The messengers deliver Vasishtha's summons. Bharata asks after everyone at home, then takes leave of his grandfather, the king of Kekaya, who sends him off with rich gifts.

ramayana-2-64-11.translation: Told this, Bharata said to the messengers, 'I will take leave of the great king; the messengers are hurrying me.'
ramayana-2-64-11.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 64: The messengers deliver Vasishtha's summons. Bharata asks after everyone at home, then takes leave of his grandfather, the king of Kekaya, who sends him off with rich gifts.

ramayana-2-64-12.translation: Having spoken thus to the messengers, Prince Bharata, urged by them, spoke to his maternal grandfather.
ramayana-2-64-12.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 64: The messengers deliver Vasishtha's summons. Bharata asks after everyone at home, then takes leave of his grandfather, the king of Kekaya, who sends him off with rich gifts.

ramayana-2-64-13.translation: King, urged by the messengers I will go to my father. I will come again whenever you think of me.
ramayana-2-64-13.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 64: The messengers deliver Vasishtha's summons. Bharata asks after everyone at home, then takes leave of his grandfather, the king of Kekaya, who sends him off with rich gifts.

ramayana-2-64-14.translation: Addressed thus by Bharata, his grandfather the king kissed Raghava on the head and spoke kind words.
ramayana-2-64-14.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 64: The messengers deliver Vasishtha's summons. Bharata asks after everyone at home, then takes leave of his grandfather, the king of Kekaya, who sends him off with rich gifts.

ramayana-2-64-15.translation: Go, dear one, I permit you. Kaikeyi is blessed with a good son in you. Give my greetings to your mother and father, scorcher of foes.
ramayana-2-64-15.meaning: He sends Bharata off with blessings.
ramayana-2-64-15.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 64: The messengers deliver Vasishtha's summons. Bharata asks after everyone at home, then takes leave of his grandfather, the king of Kekaya, who sends him off with rich gifts.

ramayana-2-64-16.translation: '...and to the royal priest and the other excellent Brahmins, and, dear one, to your brothers Rama and Lakshmana, the great archers.'
ramayana-2-64-16.meaning: The grandfather sends greetings to all.
ramayana-2-64-16.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 64: Bharata takes leave of his grandfather and uncle in Kekaya, who load him with gifts, and sets out for Ayodhya with Shatrughna.

ramayana-2-64-17.translation: The Kekaya king honoured Bharata and gave him wealth: fine elephants, colourful blankets and deerskins.
ramayana-2-64-17.meaning: Bharata is sent off with rich gifts.
ramayana-2-64-17.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 64: Bharata takes leave of his grandfather and uncle in Kekaya, who load him with gifts, and sets out for Ayodhya with Shatrughna.

ramayana-2-64-18.translation: The Kekaya king honoured Kaikeyi's son and ordered wealth for him: two thousand gold coins and sixteen hundred horses.
ramayana-2-64-18.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 64: Bharata takes leave of his grandfather and uncle in Kekaya, who load him with gifts, and sets out for Ayodhya with Shatrughna.

ramayana-2-64-19.translation: Ashvapati also quickly gave Bharata trusted, capable and virtuous ministers to accompany him.
ramayana-2-64-19.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 64: Bharata takes leave of his grandfather and uncle in Kekaya, who load him with gifts, and sets out for Ayodhya with Shatrughna.

ramayana-2-64-20.translation: His uncle gave him as wealth handsome elephants of the Airavata and Indrashira breeds, and swift, well-trained mules.
ramayana-2-64-20.meaning: Fine animals are part of the gift.
ramayana-2-64-20.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 64: Bharata takes leave of his grandfather and uncle in Kekaya, who load him with gifts, and sets out for Ayodhya with Shatrughna.

ramayana-2-64-21.translation: He also gave as a present huge dogs raised in the inner palace, armed with fangs, with the strength and courage of tigers.
ramayana-2-64-21.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 64: Bharata takes leave of his grandfather and uncle in Kekaya, who load him with gifts, and sets out for Ayodhya with Shatrughna.

ramayana-2-64-22.translation: Taking leave of his grandfather and his uncle Yudhajit, Bharata mounted his chariot and left with Shatrughna.
ramayana-2-64-22.meaning: The brothers set out for home.
ramayana-2-64-22.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 64: Bharata takes leave of his grandfather and uncle in Kekaya, who load him with gifts, and sets out for Ayodhya with Shatrughna.

ramayana-2-64-23.translation: Servants yoked over a hundred chariots with round wheels and followed Bharata with camels, oxen, horses and mules.
ramayana-2-64-23.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 64: Bharata takes leave of his grandfather and uncle in Kekaya, who load him with gifts, and sets out for Ayodhya with Shatrughna.

ramayana-2-64-24.translation: Protected by an army, with ministers as dear as himself from his grandfather, great-souled Bharata, free of enemies, took Shatrughna and left the house like a perfected being leaving Indra's world.
ramayana-2-64-24.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 64: Bharata takes leave of his grandfather and uncle in Kekaya, who load him with gifts, and sets out for Ayodhya with Shatrughna.

ramayana-2-65-1.translation: Setting out eastward from Rajagriha, the mighty and glorious joy of the Ikshvakus crossed the river Hradini, with far banks, and the Shatadru, its waves flowing westward.
ramayana-2-65-1.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 65: Bharata's journey home over many rivers and forests takes seven nights. Approaching Ayodhya, he finds it silent and joyless and sees many bad omens. He enters his father's palace with a heavy heart.

ramayana-2-65-2.translation: Crossing the river at Eladhana and reaching Aparaparpata, he crossed the Shila and Akurvati and came to Agneya and Shalyakartana.
ramayana-2-65-2.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 65: Bharata's journey home over many rivers and forests takes seven nights. Approaching Ayodhya, he finds it silent and joyless and sees many bad omens. He enters his father's palace with a heavy heart.

ramayana-2-65-3.translation: True to his word, pure and glorious, gazing at the Shilavaha, he passed great mountains towards the Chaitraratha forest.
ramayana-2-65-3.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 65: Bharata's journey home over many rivers and forests takes seven nights. Approaching Ayodhya, he finds it silent and joyless and sees many bad omens. He enters his father's palace with a heavy heart.

ramayana-2-65-4.translation: Reaching the swift Kulinga, roaring and hemmed in by hills, and the Yamuna, he crossed and then rested his army.
ramayana-2-65-4.meaning: He crosses the Yamuna and rests.
ramayana-2-65-4.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 65: Bharata's journey home over many rivers and forests takes seven nights. Approaching Ayodhya, he finds it silent and joyless and sees many bad omens. He enters his father's palace with a heavy heart.

ramayana-2-65-5.translation: Cooling their limbs and refreshing the tired horses, bathing and drinking there, he went on carrying water.
ramayana-2-65-5.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 65: Bharata's journey home over many rivers and forests takes seven nights. Approaching Ayodhya, he finds it silent and joyless and sees many bad omens. He enters his father's palace with a heavy heart.

ramayana-2-65-6.translation: The noble prince crossed the great, seldom-visited forest in his fine chariot as the wind crosses the sky.
ramayana-2-65-6.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 65: Bharata's journey home over many rivers and forests takes seven nights. Approaching Ayodhya, he finds it silent and joyless and sees many bad omens. He enters his father's palace with a heavy heart.

ramayana-2-65-7.translation: By the southern side of Torana he reached Jambuprastha, and the son of Dasharatha went on to the lovely village of Varutha.
ramayana-2-65-7.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 65: Bharata's journey home over many rivers and forests takes seven nights. Approaching Ayodhya, he finds it silent and joyless and sees many bad omens. He enters his father's palace with a heavy heart.

ramayana-2-65-8.translation: Staying there in a lovely forest, he went east to the garden of Ujjihana, where there are priyaka trees.
ramayana-2-65-8.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 65: Bharata's journey home over many rivers and forests takes seven nights. Approaching Ayodhya, he finds it silent and joyless and sees many bad omens. He enters his father's palace with a heavy heart.

ramayana-2-65-9.translation: Reaching the sala and priyaka trees, Bharata took swift horses, left instructions for the army, and went on quickly.
ramayana-2-65-9.meaning: He hurries ahead of his army.
ramayana-2-65-9.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 65: Bharata's journey home over many rivers and forests takes seven nights. Approaching Ayodhya, he finds it silent and joyless and sees many bad omens. He enters his father's palace with a heavy heart.

ramayana-2-65-10.translation: Staying at Sarvatirtha and crossing the Uttanaka river and many other rivers with mountain horses...
ramayana-2-65-10.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 65: Bharata's journey home over many rivers and forests takes seven nights. Approaching Ayodhya, he finds it silent and joyless and sees many bad omens. He enters his father's palace with a heavy heart.

ramayana-2-65-11.translation: Reaching Hastiprishthaka, he passed Kutika. The tiger among men crossed the Kapivati at Lauhitya, the Sthanumati at Ekasala and the Gomati at Vinata.
ramayana-2-65-11.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 65: Bharata's journey home over many rivers and forests takes seven nights. Approaching Ayodhya, he finds it silent and joyless and sees many bad omens. He enters his father's palace with a heavy heart.

ramayana-2-65-12.translation: Reaching the sala forest at the town of Kalinga, Bharata came quickly, his horses utterly exhausted.
ramayana-2-65-12.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 65: Bharata's journey home over many rivers and forests takes seven nights. Approaching Ayodhya, he finds it silent and joyless and sees many bad omens. He enters his father's palace with a heavy heart.

ramayana-2-65-13.translation: Quickly crossing the forest, at dawn after the night, he saw Ayodhya, built by King Manu.
ramayana-2-65-13.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 65: Bharata's journey home over many rivers and forests takes seven nights. Approaching Ayodhya, he finds it silent and joyless and sees many bad omens. He enters his father's palace with a heavy heart.

ramayana-2-65-14.translation: Having spent seven nights on the road, the tiger among men saw the city of Ayodhya ahead and spoke to the charioteer in the chariot.
ramayana-2-65-14.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 65: Bharata's journey home over many rivers and forests takes seven nights. Approaching Ayodhya, he finds it silent and joyless and sees many bad omens. He enters his father's palace with a heavy heart.

ramayana-2-65-15.translation: Charioteer, this glorious Ayodhya with its holy gardens and pale soil, seen from afar, does not look quite itself to me.
ramayana-2-65-15.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 65: Bharata's journey home over many rivers and forests takes seven nights. Approaching Ayodhya, he finds it silent and joyless and sees many bad omens. He enters his father's palace with a heavy heart.

ramayana-2-65-16.translation: ...the city full of worshippers, virtuous Brahmins learned in the Vedas, and wealthy people, protected by the best of royal sages.
ramayana-2-65-16.meaning: He recalls the city's usual life.
ramayana-2-65-16.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 65: Bharata's journey home over many rivers and forests takes seven nights. Approaching Ayodhya, he finds it silent and joyless and sees many bad omens. He enters his father's palace with a heavy heart.

ramayana-2-65-17.translation: In Ayodhya, a great, loud noise of men and women used to be heard all around. Today I do not hear it.
ramayana-2-65-17.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 65: Bharata's journey home over many rivers and forests takes seven nights. Approaching Ayodhya, he finds it silent and joyless and sees many bad omens. He enters his father's palace with a heavy heart.

ramayana-2-65-18.translation: At other times the gardens shone in the evening with people running about everywhere after playing.
ramayana-2-65-18.explanation: Ayodhya Kanda, chapter 65: Bharata's journey home over many rivers and forests takes seven nights. Approaching Ayodhya, he finds it silent and joyless and sees many bad omens. He enters his father's palace with a heavy heart.

ramayana-2-65-19.translation: Today, abandoned by pleasure-seekers, they seem to weep. Charioteer, the city seems to me like a wilderness.
